headline: Forget the Fluke — Bunker Are Getting Squeezed at the Inlet and the Bass Know It
subhead: The new moon tide is stacking bait against the jetty rocks, and the first real blitz of the fall run is lining up right at Jones Inlet.
body_markdown:
Everybody and their cousin is still out there drifting Sloop Channel for fluke like it's the Fourth of July. Skip it this week. The fluke game inshore is running out of gas — most of what's coming over the rail in the bay right now is short fish, the kind you measure twice and toss back disappointed. The better fluke already made their move to deeper, cooler water offshore, which is the normal September shuffle, but it means your time is better spent somewhere else. And that somewhere else is the inlet mouth, where the real story of the week is playing out.

That new moon that came through on the 10th put a big tidal push behind everything happening out here, and it's doing exactly what a hard new-moon tide is supposed to do this time of year — squeezing bunker pods tight against the beach and jamming them right up against the rocks at the east and west jetties. We flagged this coming last week — said the building tide would tighten those pods and light off the first real bass blitz of the season at the inlet mouth — and that's precisely what's setting up right now. The bunker have nowhere to go when that current funnels them against structure, and stripers know it. They're starting to commit hard instead of just picking at stragglers, which is the difference between a fall run that's talked about and one that's fished.

Ocean side has been a little beat up — offshore buoys are reading better than 3-foot swell on a short period, which means the open beach off Jones has had some size and push to it, not the glass-calm conditions you want for reading bait from the sand. That chop has done one useful thing though: it's pushed the bait and the bass that are chasing it into the calmer, current-driven water inside the inlet and along the protected stretches of Short Beach. If you're picking your spot this week, that's the tell. Skip the exposed beach when there's swell running and work the inlet mouth, the jetty rocks, and the mouth of the channels where the water's still moving but not getting hammered by ocean energy.

The pattern to fish is the outgoing tide, full stop. As that new-moon ebb drains the back bay and the marsh creeks around Hempstead Bay and South Oyster Bay, it's pulling warm, bait-rich water right out through the inlet and dumping it into a tightening current seam where the bass are waiting. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, 3 to 4 ounces depending on how hard the water's ripping, cast right into that seam off the east jetty at Jones Inlet, has been the go-to for guys getting into keeper-class bass in the 28- to 34-inch range on the last two hours of the ebb into dead low. If you want to work it artificial, a bunker-spoon or a big white paddletail swimbait, 6 to 8 inches, worked slow through the wash where the current pushes against the rocks, has been drawing strikes from fish that are clearly locked onto peanut and adult bunker both.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on this whole pattern and they're not subtle about it. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay canals around Freeport and up toward the Wantagh Bridge, which tells you the bigger cousins aren't far behind — that's the usual sequence this time of year, snappers first, then the adults show up hungry once the water eases another few degrees. Anybody working topwater poppers or small metal off the jetty rocks at first light should expect company from blues mixed right in with the bass, and that's not a bad problem to have when the bunker are getting torn up on the surface.

Weakfish are still a side note but worth mentioning because they're actually showing up again in the deeper holes of the bay, something this fishery hasn't had much of in years. Guys jigging bucktails tipped with a strip of squid or bunker along the drop-offs near the Wantagh Bridge channel edges on the last of the incoming have been picking off a few keeper weakfish mixed in with the fluke. It's not a bite you plan a whole trip around yet, but it's a real sign the population's coming back, and it's worth a few casts if you're already out there working the tide change.

Looking at the next few days, the tidal push from this new moon isn't done working. Expect the blitz activity at the inlet mouth to build over the next 48 hours as the bunker pods get squeezed even tighter and more bass commit to the school instead of just shadowing it. That window should hold through the week before easing up as the moon pulls away from new phase and the tidal energy backs off a notch. If you've only got one shot this weekend, make it the outgoing tide at first light off the east jetty — that's where the bait, the current, and the bass are all lining up at once. Keep an eye on the ocean swell too; if it lays down even a little, the open beach stretches around Jones Beach and Short Beach could turn on with blitzing bass working bunker right in the wash, which is the kind of surf bite this whole run is building toward.
